name: Candle business
blurb: Make scented candles at home and sell them online, at markets or to local shops
title: How to Start a Candle Business: Costs, Safety and Risks
description: How to start a candle business: how it makes money, supplies, burn testing and labelling rules, who it suits, the risks and how to test before you sell.
h1: How to start a candle business
answer: A candle business makes candles, usually scented ones in jars or tins, and sells them online, at craft markets, or wholesale to gift shops. You earn the gap between your price and wax, fragrance, wicks, containers, packaging and shipping. The catch is that candles are a fire and allergy risk, so you must test every recipe and meet safety and labelling rules, and the market is crowded with similar products.

sections.h: How a candle business makes money
body: You sell per candle, in gift sets, or in bulk to shops and event planners at a lower wholesale price. Custom candles for weddings or corporate gifts can carry higher prices.

Materials are only part of the cost. Testing batches, failed pours, glass breakage in shipping, marketplace fees, market stall fees and your time all come out of the margin. Branding and scent choice largely decide what you can charge.

ul: Wax, wicks, fragrance oils made for candles, containers, a thermometer, a scale and a heat source; start with a small kit.
A safe workspace with ventilation and fire safety equipment.
A burn-testing routine: test each wax, wick and fragrance combination before selling it.

Warning and safety labels. In Great Britain and the EU, scented candles count as chemical mixtures under CLP rules, so some fragrance ingredients require allergy warnings and hazard symbols on the label; other countries have their own product safety and labelling rules.
Product liability insurance, which shops and markets often ask for.
Business registration and tax setup; check local rules.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Careful makers who enjoy testing and record-keeping
Anyone who wants to skip burn tests
People with a strong eye for branding and photos
People with no safe space to work with hot wax
Sellers with access to craft markets or local gift shops
Anyone expecting candles to stand out without a clear style

ul: Fire and injury: a wrong wick size can cause large flames, soot or overheated glass. Untested candles create real liability.
Labelling: missing allergen warnings or safety instructions can break product safety rules where you sell.
Saturation: many small candle brands look and smell similar, so marketing costs rise.
Shipping: glass and wax can break or melt in transit; test your packaging.
Seasonality: gift seasons bring peaks and quieter months follow.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Buy a small starter set of supplies rather than bulk wax and fragrance.
Pour a few test candles and burn-test them fully, recording flame size, soot and container heat.
Give finished candles to friends and ask what they would pay and whether they would buy again.
Visit local markets and gift shops to see what similar candles cost.
Cost one candle fully, including failed batches, labels, packaging and shipping.
Register the business, arrange product liability insurance and check the labelling rules where you will sell.
Settle on a small range of tested scents and one container style.
Design labels with your details, safety instructions and any required allergen statements.
Sell at one market or through one online shop and collect feedback.
Keep batch records so you can trace any problem back to the materials used.

faq.q: Do I need a licence to sell candles?
faq.a: There is rarely a candle-specific licence, but you usually need business registration, and candles must meet product safety and labelling rules where they are sold. Insurance is strongly advised. Check local rules.

faq.q: What wax is best for a candle business?
faq.a: Soy, coconut blends, paraffin and beeswax all behave differently with fragrance and wicks. Pick one, learn it through testing, and be honest in your descriptions rather than relying on vague "clean burning" claims.

faq.q: Can I sell candles on Etsy or other marketplaces?
faq.a: Yes, handmade candles are commonly sold on marketplaces. Read each platform's rules for handmade items and make sure your labels and safety information are complete.
